## My Thinking

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. The North China Plain is a wheat-corn country — everyone here knows that. The soil is good loam, the government subsidizes both crops, and I have reliable market access. There's no reason to gamble on something unfamiliar at my age, and the double-cropping system (winter wheat followed by summer maize) uses the land efficiently through both seasons.

My biggest concern is water. Quzhou is sitting on a depleted aquifer and the county has been tightening groundwater quotas for years. I've watched neighbors ruin their margins paying for extra pumping. So I'll irrigate less than the old way — I'll push the wheat to 3 irrigations maximum, timed carefully at overwintering, jointing, and heading. For maize I'll rely on summer rains and irrigate only if I really need to.

I have about 15 mu under cultivation. My education means I follow the county agricultural extension recommendations closely and I buy improved certified seed every season rather than saving my own. For wheat I'll use Jimai 22 or Shimai 15 — well-adapted to southern Hebei, disease-tolerant, decent yield. For summer maize I'll go hybrid, probably Xianyu 335 or Zhengdan 958 — proven performers here. I won't chase the newest hybrid varieties every year; that's a young man's gamble.

On fertilizer, I'll apply base phosphorus and potassium at planting for both crops, and split the nitrogen — base plus a top-dress — because I've seen what over-fertilizing does to the soil and the runoff. I use no-till direct seeding for maize right into the wheat stubble to save time and reduce erosion. For wheat I'll do rotary tillage since the ground needs it after the dry summer.

I'll handle pesticides myself: pre-emergence herbicide and one fungicide pass for the wheat, a single herbicide/insecticide pass for the maize. Nothing excessive.
